plain_english:
"But how can this man call himself a philosopher when he lives like a rich man? He says wealth should be despised — yet he has it. He says life should be despised — yet he goes on living. He says health should be despised — yet he takes the best possible care of himself. He calls exile meaningless — 'What's so bad about moving to another country?' — and yet, given the choice, he grows old at home. He says it makes no difference whether life is long or short — and yet, if nothing stops him, he lives as long as he can, thriving well into old age."

His answer is this: these things should be despised, yes — but that doesn't mean he shouldn't have them. It means he shouldn't cling to them in fear. He doesn't push them away. But when they leave, he lets them go without fuss. And really, where could fortune store its riches more safely than with someone who will hand them back without an argument?
original_excerpt:
"But how is it that this man studies philosophy and nevertheless
lives the life of a rich man? Why does he say that wealth ought to
be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and
yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the
utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible? Does he consider
banishment to be an empty name, and say, "What evil is there in
changing one country for another?" and yet, if permitted, does he
not grow old in his native land? does he declare that there is no
difference between a longer and a shorter time, and yet, if he be
not prevented, lengthen out his life and flourish in a green old
age?" His answer is, that these things ought to be despised, not
that he should not possess them, but that he should not possess
them with fear and trembling: he does not drive them away from him,
but when they leave him he follows after them unconcernedly. Where,
indeed, can fortune invest riches more securely than in a place
from whence they can always be recovered without any squabble with
their trustee?

plain_english: Marcus Cato used to praise Curius and Coruncanius, and that whole generation when owning a few small silver coins was enough to get you punished by the Censor. Yet Cato himself owned four million sesterces. Less than Crassus, sure — but far more than his great-grandfather, Cato the Censor. Compare the numbers: he had outpaced his great-grandfather by a wider margin than Crassus had outpaced him. And if even greater wealth had come his way, he wouldn't have turned it down. A wise person doesn't consider themselves above whatever luck sends their way. They don't love money, but they'd rather have it than not. They don't take it into their soul — only into their house. They don't throw away what they already have. They keep it, and they're glad to give their character a bigger stage to prove itself on.
original_excerpt:
Marcus Cato, when he was praising Curius and Coruncanius
and that century in which the possession of a few small silver coins
were an offence which was punished by the Censor, himself owned
four million sesterces; a less fortune no doubt, than that
of Crassus, but larger than of Cato the Censor. If the amounts be
compared, he had outstripped his great-grandfather further than he
himself was outdone by Crassus, and if still greater riches had
fallen to his lot, he would not have spurned them: for the wise man
does not think himself unworthy of any chance presents: he does not
love riches, but he prefers to have them; he does not receive them
into his spirit, but only into his house: nor does he cast away
from him what he already possesses, but keeps them, and is willing
that his virtue should receive a larger subject-matter for its
exercise.
